claims.text: Greg Short asserts that undivided attention produces sharper decisions and smoother, faster execution — the implication being that splitting attention across multiple pursuits degrades both decision quality and speed of output.
claims.speaker: Greg Short

claims.text: Greg Short argues that when someone commits to pursuing a goal, they should target something very large rather than something merely achievable, on the grounds that the required effort and sacrifice are largely fixed regardless of ambition level.
claims.speaker: Greg Short

claims.text: Greg Short asserts that pursuing greatness requires consciously giving up good options — the trade is real and expected to feel uncomfortable, and people in the social circle of the person pursuing it will likely label the choice as irrational.
claims.speaker: Greg Short

claims.text: Greg Short observes that ambitious early-stage pursuit predictably generates social pressure: people around the pursuer will characterize the goal as crazy, and the pursuer should reframe this by naming youth and desire for broader impact (family, team, community) as justification rather than seeking approval.
claims.speaker: Greg Short

practices.text: When peers or family push back on an ambitious goal, respond by naming that you are young and want more for yourself, your family, your team, and your community — make the motivation explicit rather than defending the goal on its merits.
If you are going to pursue a goal, pursue something large enough to be worth the sacrifice; do not dilute ambition by targeting something merely attainable.
